readings.c1s1:
¶

'''apheretically''' (af-e-ret′i-kạl-i), ''adv.'' After the manner of an apheresis; by omitting the first syllable. Also spelled ''aphæretically.''

'''aphesis''' (af′e-sis), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἄφεσις, a letting go, let go, let loose, < ἀφιέναι, let go, send off, < ἀπό, off, + ἱέναι, send.] The gradual and unintentional removal of a short unaccented vowel at the beginning of a word; a special form of apheresis, as in ''squire'' for ''esquire, down'' for ''adown'', etc. ''J. A. H. Murray.'' (''N. E. D.'')

'''apheta''' (af′e-tä̤), ''n.'' [ML., < Gr. ἀφέτης, one who lets go, hence one who lets go a military engine, and, according to Du Cange, one who starts the chariots in a race (cf. ἀφετηρία, the starting-place, MGr. ἀφετοθυρανοίκτης, one who opened the barriers to start the racing-chariots), hence in astrology the planet which starts a human being in his career, < ἄφετος, let off, let loose, verbal adj. of ἀφιέναι, let off: see ''aphesis.''] In ''astrol.'', the planet dominating the life of the native; the planet which is lord of the house that rules the matter inquired after; the prorogator, significator, or hyleg.
{{smaller block|The aphetic place is the situation of the ''Apheta'', Hyleg, prorogator, significator, or giver of life, for they all have the same meaning.
{{right|''Sibley'', Astrology, p. 433.}}}}

'''apheter''' (af′e-tėr), ''n.'' [< Gr. ἀφετήρ, equiv. to ἀφέτης, one who lets off a military engine: see ''apheta.''] That which loosens or sets free. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|This katastate is, as it were, the fuse or trigger whose action fires the massive charge of the muscular gun, and might receive the name of ''apheter.''
{{right|''M. Foster'', Encyc. Brit., XIX. 20.}}}}

'''aphetic<sup>1</sup>''' (a-fet′ik), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἀφετικός, < ἄφετος, let loose, set free: see ''aphesis'' and ''apheta.''] Produced by or resulting from aphesis.

'''aphetic<sup>2</sup>''' (a-fet′ik), ''a.'' [< ''apheta'' + ''-ic.''] Same as ''aphetical.''

'''aphetical''' (a-fet′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' [< ''aphetic''<sup>2</sup> + ''-al.''] In ''astrol.'', pertaining to the apheta, or planet significative of life.—{{smaller|'''Aphetical places''' (translation of Greek τόποι ἀφετικοί), the places in which the apheta may be found. The rules given in Ptolemy’s “Tetrabiblos” (iii. 10) are intricate and vague.}}

'''aphetically<sup>1</sup>''' (a-fet′i-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an aphetic manner.

'''aphetically<sup>2</sup>''' (a-fet′i-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In the manner or position of the apheta.

'''aphetism''' (af′e-tizm), ''n.'' [< ''aphetic''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ism.''] An aphetized form of a word; a form resulting from the loss of a weak initial vowel, as ''down'' for ''adown.''

'''aphetize''' (af′e-tīz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''aphetized'', ppr. ''aphetizing.'' [< ''aphetic''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ize.''] To render aphetic; shorten by aphesis.

'''aphid''' (af′id), ''n.'' [< ''aphis'' (''aphid-'').] An aphidian; a plant-louse; a member of the genus ''Aphis'' or family ''Aphididæ'' (which see). In the plural, the plant-lice: a general or indeterminate term for the members (''a'') of the genus

''Aphis'', (''b'') of the family ''Aphididæ'', or (''c'') of the suborder ''Phytophthiria''.

'''Aphides''' (af′i-dēz), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of ''Aphis'', q. v.] Same as ''Aphididæ''.

'''aphidian''' (a-fid′i-ạn), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ''Aphis'' (''Aphid-'') + ''-ian''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' An insect of the family ''Aphididæ''; an aphid; a plant-louse.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to the genus ''Aphis'' or to the family ''Aphididæ''.

'''aphidid''' (af′i-did), ''n.'' One of the ''Aphididæ''; an aphis.
{{smaller block|The Fenesica larva actually feeds upon the ''aphidids''.
{{right|''Science'', VII. 394.}}}}

'''Aphididæ''' (a-fid′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Aphis'' (''Aphid-'') + ''-idæ''.] A family of hemipterous insects, of the suborder ''Phytophthiria''; the true plant-lice, as typified by the genus ''Aphis'', and as distinguished from the false plant-lice, or ''Psyllidæ'', and other phytophthirian insects. {{smaller|They are all injurious to vegetation, living on the juices of plants, which they suck, and also producing a great variety of galls. Almost every plant has lice peculiar to it, immense numbers of which live upon it. The genera are very numerous. See cuts under ''Aphis''. Also called ''Aphides''.}}

'''Aphidii''' (a-fid′i-ī), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of ''aphidius'' (also used to designate a genus of hymenopterous insects), < ''Aphis'' (''Aphid-''), q. v.] In Latreille’s system of classification, the second

family of homopterous hemipterous insects, commonly called plant-lice, inexactly equivalent to the modern family ''Aphididæ'', including the thysanurous genus ''Thrips'', etc., as well as the ''Psyllidæ'' or false plant-lice, and excluding the ''Coccidæ'' or scale-insects. [Not in use.]

'''aphidious''' (a-fid′i-us), ''a.'' [< ''aphid'' + ''-ious.''] Pertaining to or of the nature of aphids.

'''Aphidiphagi''' (af-i-dif′ạ-jī), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of ''aphidiphagus'': see ''aphidiphagous''.] In Latreille’s system of classification, the second family of trimerous ''Coleoptera'', consisting of the old genus ''Coccinella'', and corresponding to the modern family ''Coccinellidæ''; the lady-birds; small beetles which habitually feed upon aphids. [Not in use.]

'''aphidiphagous''' (af-i-dif′ạ-gus), ''a.'' [< NL. ''aphidiphagus'', < ''Aphis'' (''Aphid-'') + Gr. -φαγος, < φαγεῖν, eat.] Of or pertaining to the ''Aphidiphaga''; hence, preying upon or devouring aphids.

'''aphidivorous''' (af-i-div′ọ̄-rus), ''a.'' [< NL. ''Aphis'' (''Aphid-'') + L. ''vorare'', devour.] Same as ''aphidiphagous''.

'''aphilanthropy''' (af-i-lan′thrọ̄-pi), ''n.'' [< Gr. ἀφιλάνθρωπος, not loving man, < ἀ- priv. + φιλάνθρωπος, loving man: see ''philanthropy''.] '''1.''' Want of philanthropy; lack of benevolence. [Rare.] —'''2.''' In ''pathol.'', preference of solitude to society, the first stage of melancholia.

'''aphnology''' (af-nol′ọ̄-ji), ''n.'' [< Gr. ἄφνος, usually ἄφενος, revenue, riches, wealth, abundance (cf. Skt. ''apnas'', income, property; akin to L. ''opes'', wealth, ''copia'', plenty, etc.), + -''λογία'', < ''λέγειν'', speak: see ''-ology''.] The science of wealth; a treatise on the science of wealth; plutology. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The title ought to have been ''Aphnology.'' Aphnos, or aphenos, expresses wealth in the largest sense of general abundance and well-being.
{{right|''Sir J. Herschel.''}}}}

'''Aphodiidæ''' (af-ō-dī′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Aphodius'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of beetles, named by Macleay in 1819 from the genus ''Aphodius''.
readings.c3s1:

'''Aphodius''' (a-fō′di-us), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἄφοδος, excrement, evacuation, and lit. departure, < ἀπό, from, away, + ὁδός, way.] A genus of scarabæoid lamellicorn beetles, related to the dung-beetles of the genus ''Geotrupes'', sometimes giving name to a family ''Aphodiidæ''. {{smaller|Its species are mostly small, having striate elytra, concealed metathoracic epimera, toothed front tibiæ and spurred hind tibiæ, and 9-jointed antennæ. Over 50 North American species are described, including several introduced from Europe, such as the comparatively large black ''A. fossor''.}}

'''Aphododeridæ''' (af″ọ-dọ-der′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' See ''Aphredoderidæ''.

'''Aphododerus''' (af-ọ-dod′e̤-rus), ''n.'' See ''Aphredoderus''.

'''aphonia''' (a-fō′ni-ä), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀφωνία, speechlessness, < ἄφωνος, speechless, voiceless: see ''aphonous''.] In ''pathol.'', loss of voice through a morbid condition of the larynx or its immediate innervation; dumbness; speechlessness. {{smaller|It is a condition in which one wants to speak and knows how to do so, but cannot produce a vocal sound, though he may whisper. Also ''aphony''.}}

'''aphonic''' (a-fon′ik), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''aphonia'' + ''-ic''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to or characterized by aphonia; speechless; dumb.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A person affected with aphonia.

'''aphonous''' (af′ọ-nus), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἄφωνος, voiceless, < ἀ- priv. + φωνή, voice: see ''phonic''.] Destitute of voice; voiceless.

'''aphony''' (af′ọ-ni), ''n.'' Same as ''aphonia''.

'''aphoria''' (a-fō′ri-ä), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀφορία, sterility, dearth, < ἄφορος, not bearing, < ἀ- priv. + φορός, bearing, < φέρειν = E. ''bear''<sup>1</sup>.] Sterility; unfruitfulness.

'''aphorism''' (af′ō̤-rizm), ''n.''   [= F. ''aphorisme'', < Gr. ἀφορισμός, a definition, a short pithy sentence, < ἀφορίζειν, define, mark off, < ἀπό, off, + ὁρίζειν, divide, bound, < ὅρος, a boundary: see ''horizon.'']   '''1.''' A definition or concise statement of a principle.
{{smaller block|The ''aphorism'' . . . formulated by Linnæus in regard to plants.
{{right|''Quatrefages'', Human Species (trans.), p. 50.}}}}
'''2.''' A precept or rule expressed in few words; a detached sentence containing some important truth: as, the ''aphorisms'' of Hippocrates, or of the civil law.
{{smaller block|The three ancient commentators on Hippocrates . . . have given the same definition of an ''aphorism'', ''i. e.'', “a succinct saying, comprehending a complete statement,” or a saying poor in expression, but rich in sentiment.
{{right|''Fleming.''}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Aphorism'', ''Axiom'', ''Maxim'', ''Precept'', ''Dictum'', ''Apothegm'', ''Saying'', ''Adage'', ''Proverb'', ''Truism'', ''Byword'', ''Saw'', all concur in expressing a pithy general proposition, usually in one short sentence; but the longer the form the less applicable do these names become. An ''aphorism'' is a truth, pointedly set forth, relating rather to speculative principles, ethics, or science than to practical matters, and forming a brief and excellent statement of a doctrine: thus, “Moderation is the silken string running through the pearl-chain of all virtues,” and “Maladies are cured by nature, not by remedies,” are ''aphorisms''. “Life is short, and art is long,” is from the first ''aphorism'' of Hippocrates. An ''axiom'' is a self-evident truth, and therefore used as a basis for reasoning. “A straight line is the shortest distance between two points” is one of the ''axioms'' of mathematics; “The greater good is to be chosen before the less” is an ''axiom'' of morals. The number of axioms is necessarily limited; of aphorisms, maxims, etc., unlimited. A ''maxim'' is a truth which, while not so definite and necessarily true as an ''axiom'', yet equally acceptable to the mind, refers rather to practical than to abstract truth, stating one of the fundamental rules of conduct, civil government, business policy, and the like: as, it is a sound ''maxim'' that one should risk in speculation no more than he can afford to lose. It suggests a lesson more pointedly and directly than ''aphorism'', and differs from ''precept'' in that a ''precept'' is a direct injunction, whereas a ''maxim'' is a mere statement of a truth from which a ''precept'' may be deduced. It would be a ''precept'' to say, “In speculation risk no more than you can afford to lose.” A ''dictum'' is not a ''precept'', but an opinion given with authority, as from superior knowledge: as, a ''dictum'' of the critics; a ''dictum'' of Carlyle’s. An ''apothegm'', in common matters what an ''aphorism'' is in higher, is essentially a terse proposition that makes a vivid impression on the mind: thus, “In the adversity of our best friends we always find something that doth not displease us”; this is called by Dean Swift a ''maxim'', but is more properly an ''apothegm''. “Heaven helps those that help themselves,” and}}

A ''saying'' is a lower grade of ''apothegm''; each is likely to be found associated with the name of the author: as, the ''apothegms'' of Socrates; a ''saying'' of Poor Richard. Each is a felicitous expression current for its own sake, but deriving additional popularity from the celebrity of its author. “Herein is that ''saying'' true, One soweth, and another reapeth,” John iv. 37; “The little and short ''sayings'' of wise and excellent men are of great value, like the dust of gold or the least sparks of the diamond,” ''Tillotson''. ''Adage'' and ''proverb'' are habitual sayings, generally of long standing, embodying the common sense of mankind on ordinary subjects. The ''adage'' is often the more venerable by age and the more dignified in its character: as, “Necessity knows no law.” A ''saying'' may easily become an ''adage''.
